speechtext:
Right Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Acting Prime Minister). The hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank) indicated on Friday that he intended to-day to bring up the question of the supply of wooden containers for food in British Columbia the production of which is rendered impossible by the strike of those engaged in making lumber for boxes and material, for baskets and other wooden food containers.
I understand that if these containers are not produced the result will be a large wastage and spoilage of food of many kinds produced in British Columbia both for the Canadian market and the overseas market during the coming months. I understand also that there is a disposition on the part of both operators and members of the unions to recognize the gravity of this situation and that meetings are being held, at least between the farmers and the workers, with a view to putting an end to this lamentable situation.
As the house knows, the importance of food at the present time is of great concern to the government, and I would like to say on behalf of the government that it is the sincere hope

Grain Crop
and wish of the government that arrangements be immediately made whereby the industry making material for wooden food containers will resume work at once, without prejudice to any negotiations regarding conditions in the industry which are now proceeding.
The Minister of Labour is unavoidably absent from the house to-day but I know that this is his wish as well as that of the other members of the government, and I am therefore, on behalf of the government, making this earnest appeal to all those concerned in this dispute to arrange for the resumption of work at once in the lumber mills which make lumber for containers for the shipping of fish and fruit and other food products.
I am not now dealing with the other phases of the strike in British Columbia, which are very grave. I will have to leave these for the Minister of Labour, who is putting forward every possible effort to bring about the settlement of the dispute as a whole.

On behalf of the Canadian wheat board I wish to make a brief statement regarding the 1944 barley equalization payments and the 1944 Ontario wheat equalization fund.
We are at present in process of making payment to all producers who delivered barley either through country elevators or by farm-to-farm transactions in the crop year 1944-45. An amount totalling $6,106,932.94 is involved in this payment, being the difference between the advance equalization payment and the equalization fees collected in respect of barley exported, after allowing for administrative costs and the estimated cost of making the payment. The payment covers deliveries made between August 1, 1944 and July 31, 1945, inclusive. In the case of deliveries through country elevators, the cheques are compiled from information submitted to the board by the handling companies. Where producers made deliveries to more than one elevator, separate cheques will be issued, one for each of the companies to whom deliveries were made. The cheques will be forwarded to the elevator companies for distribution when completed, but cheques covering the farm-to-farm transactions will be distributed by mail from the offices of the board.

deliveries of 80,435,781 bushels, and the amount per bushel of the payment is 7-59 cents.
Immediately following completion of the barley payment, payment will be made to the producers who delivered Ontario winter wheat in the 1944-45 crop year. This payment will be made on the basis of monthly reports received from the elevator agents in the province of Ontario. The surplus arising as a result of the equalization fees collected in Ontario winter flour and other wheat products exported from that crop, after allowing for administrative costs and the estimated cost of making the payment, totals $192,824.77. The current advertisements sponsored by the Department of Trade and Commerce are of two kinds: (a) addressed through newspapers and magazines to the public on the general theme "One Third of Your Dollar"- the proportion of our national income conservatively estimated as earned, directly or indirectly, by export trade. These advertisements are designed to bring home to Canadians generally, in addition to producers and exporters, the importance of foreign trade to their daily lives. The advertisements further point out that in order to build up our export trade now it would be wise to do without some things in the domestic market in order that at least token shipments may be sent to markets abroad, thus enabling connections to be established that will be needed in the future; (b) addressed through business publications to actual and potential exporters on the general theme "C.Q.P."-meaning continuity of supply, quality that is consistent, prices that are fair. Good export practices are the long-term means of promoting our trade, and the advertisements are designed with that purpose in mind.
In general, therefore, the Department of Trade and Commerce is trying through its advertisements to prepare the ground at home for the maintenance of the level of export and import trade which is believed to be essential to Canada's prosperity.

speechtext:
On May 21 the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Irvine) asked this question:
Have the government any information as to the great shortage of barbed wire for fencing and, if so, what are they doing about it?
The average monthly production in Canada of barbed wire is approximately 1,000 tons. None of this is exported at.the present time. This barbed wire is distributed by the producers to the consumers through the regular trade channels namely the jobbers, distributors and hardware firms. The producers are doing their utmost to maintain equitable distribution of the available supply. To divert increased tonnages of wire for this product would merely result in taking the steel away from some other product which is equally urgent and in equally short supply. For example, it could veiy possibly affect the production of nails, another wire mill product. The short supply of barbed wire is merely one part of our overall acute steel supply position. The condition here is no more acute than the supply position of plate, structural, sheet bars, rods and all wire mill products.

Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Reconstruction and Supply) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to bring in a measure to amend the Research Council Act to provide for the continuance of the committee of the privy council on industrial and scientific research; for the appointment of two vice-presidents to the research council, their tenure of office and salaries; for the appointment of an executvie committee of the council; for the creation of corporations to carry out certain powers of the council which may be more conveniently performed by a separate corporation, and also to provide for the organization, administration and financing of such corporations; and to provide further for the superannuation pension and, other rights of the employees of the said corporations.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF VICE-PRESIDENTS AND EXECUTIVE COMMITTEE, ETC.
speechtext: May I ask the minister whether it is his intention to make a statement with regard to this resolution?

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF VICE-PRESIDENTS AND EXECUTIVE COMMITTEE, ETC.
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker. The present Research Council Act was passed in 1924, and has not been amended since. On the other hand, as everyone knows, the research council has expanded greatly since that date in order to meet the needs of Canada in this technological age, and the present amendments are being proposed in order to bring the formal organizational structure of the council into harmony with its present day activities.

Research Council
Before discussing details of the proposed amendments, I would like to indicate in very broad terms the great changes that have taken place in the scope of the council's work since 1928. In that year a full-time president, Dr. Troy, was appointed, and a decision was taken to provide a research laboratory building. Previously the activities of the council had been confined to awarding scholarships, making financial grants in aid of research to university and other workers, and organizing cooperative research projects. The council's budget in 1928-29 was $323,366.56. In 1932 the main research building on Sussex street was formally opened. For the fiscal year 1932-33 the council's budget was approximately $450,000, and the professional staff numbered 57. For the fiscal year before the war, that is 1938-39, the council's budget increased to approximately $1,000,000, and there was a total staff of a little less than 300.
During the war, as we all know, the council's activities expanded greatly in magnitude and diversity, and during the last year of the war the council was supporting directly a total staff of 1,600, and indirectly another 400. The total direct expenditures amounted to nearly $7 million., or seven times the 1938-39 figure. And, in addition, the president and other administrative officers of the council carried scientific responsibilities for operations such as the atomic energy project, and many other secret operations supported financially by the Department of Munitions and Supply and the Department of National Defence, which ran into many millions of dollars. All this expansion took place without any permanent change or additions in the permanent administrative staff.
The government has decided that the peacetime needs for scientific research in Canada require that the activities of the research council be maintained on the same order of magnitude as in war, and in the estimates for the current fiscal year the needs of the council are placed at about $6,378,000, which is apart from the very sizable expenditures on atomic energy activties which are directed by the president and administrative officers of the council.
Compared with the staff of 300 in 1939, the full-time civilian staff will number about 1,500. In addition to the one large laboratory bhild-ing of 1939, the council is now operating sixteen other laboratories in Ottawa, in Montreal, in Chalk River, in Winnipeg, in Saskatoon, and plans have already been drawn for several others, including a building research laboratory, a road research laboratory, and a new radio and radar laboratory.
In addition to the laboratories, the president is responsible for the administration of about 50 associate research committees and 100 subcommittees, on which sit literally hundreds of the country's most distinguished scientists, engineers, and industrialists, and who in turn consider and lay down policy in connection with broad research projects such as aeronautics, Canadian government purchasing standards, medical research, explosives, geophysics, dental research, radio research and a number of others.
The council also operates scientific liaison offices in London, Washington and Ottawa, maintains a large scientific library, publishes the Canadian Journal of Research and many other reports. It has an active programme of awarding scholarships and making grants in aid of research-all of which have increased during the past few years in the same proportion as the other activities.
The president of the council acts as adviser to the government on an increasing number of scientific subjects, sits on a large number of boards and committees of a general character, has assumed the responsibilities of director-general of the research and development branch of the Department of Reconstruction and Supply, is proposed as a member of the atomic energy board to be set up, and also acts as a special adviser and consultant in connection with military research-all of which, it will be seen, represents a greatly increased administrative burden as compared to the organizations of 1932 and 1939. While the war was on, the administration of the council received help and advice from senior officials seconded from universities and from senior officers in the Department of Reconstruction and Supply, but now that such help will no longer be available, it is obvious that there is need formally to strengthen the top administrative set-up of the council by providing for two senior officials:	a vice-president (administration),
and a vice-president (scientific); and there is also need for other provisions which will be found in the proposed amendments.
The remainder of what I have to say deals with individual sections'of the bill. Perhaps that might best be said after the bill has been introduced.

Mr. Speaker, the house has before it this afternoon two of the most important resolutions we have ever considered, namely resolutions numbers 13 and 14 on the order paper. Of the two, probably the former is the more important.
Speaking briefly to this resolution, number 14, may I point out that we welcome the proposals contained in it, and look forward to the introduction of the bill. We have long been of the opinion that an expansion of our scientific activities is essential at this time. As a matter of fact, what I fear is that people in public life-political leaders, and in some degree men in charge of our defence forces- are failing to exercise, in the matter of scientific progress, that degree of imagination the scientists themselves are exercising.
I hope this resolution means that Canada will expand her scientific research in a big way, and that the scientific branch in the national research council will be comprised of our outstanding young men in science. I was amazed when I learned the ages of many of the young scientists who had been engaged in the important work to which the Minister of Reconstruction has referred. We know something of the contribution they made in the discovery and development of RDX; we know of the work they did in radar, and of the work they are doing in connection with nuclear physics.
We wholeheartedly support the idea behind the resolution, and behind the other resolution about which I shall speak at a later time. I would hope, however, that the scale of salaries we shall institute will be sufficiently attractive to secure able scientists for the public service of Canada. We have lost too many young scientists in the past to our great neighbour to the south, and in various fields they have found employment across the seas. Some of the physicists, doctors and scientists who have made names for themselves in Great Britain were graduates of Canadian universities:	I sincerely hope the scale of

salaries, the superannuation benefits and the conditions of service will be such as to attract the best of our young Canadians.
I hope that ways and means will be found also to encourage our young Canadian scientists to exchange their scientific knowledge with scientists in other countries. We cannot allow matters of defence to be betrayed when the government desires to retain them or to let them out only on a reciprocal basis, but I think there is a danger at the present time of scientific researchers being so constricted or restricted that the exchange of scientific knowledge among the nations may be interfered with to our disadvantage and to the disadvantage of the world generally.
All I intended to say at this stage is that we welcome this resolution. We believe it is a step in the right direction. It shows some forward-looking thinking on the part of the minister and his advisers, and I sincerely hope that the scientific research branch of Canada will contribute to the scientific knowledge of the world and to the development of our own great resources, primarily for the good of Canada and, of course, of the world generally.

Mr. Speaker, it gives me great satisfaction to see this resolution introduced. In Canada we are faced with two great problems. First, we must learn how to adjust ourselves to the atomic age. When the atomic bomb was first used I was afraid that the calamity howlers were going to terrify us into a state of paralysis so that w-e would not do anything about this atomic bomb but lie down and yield our national sovereignty to some international body or do all the other foolish things that were being suggested. This resolution

Research Council

indicates a determination to go right out and meet the situation; after all that is the only sensible thing to do.
I heard a story the other day about three or four soldiers who some thousands of years ago were supervising the first attack with a catapult on a walled city. When they were-all ready to shoot the first great stone with the eatapault, one of the soldiers said to his companions, "Well, this will end war all right!" I take it that this organization will direct its efforts first of all towards defending ourselves against an atomic bomb attack, and next towards the means of launching an atomic bomb attack in case we need to do so.
The other extremely important problem is one which I have not yet heard mentioned as one of the problems that would be given to a research council; considering its seriousness I am amazed that we have not long ago turned it over to a national research body. We fought the last war because men did not know how to distribute goods, and the indications are that we shall have to fight the next war because men still do not know how to distribute goods. Men do not seem to realize that distribution is a scientific problem which has to be solved by scientific means. I hope that at an early day the minister will turn over to a considerable body of scientific men the task of ascertaining how to distribute in Canada the maximum amount of goods which Canada is able to produce, so that the people of Canada will be able to enjoy the maximum standard of living which would be justified by our productive capacity. I should like to bring to his attention four or five points on which we wish to have information.
What is the policy of the government with regard to having research carried on in different parts of Canada, and how far does the government propose to go in dividing the work up to make certain that problems which affect perhaps only one or two parts of Canada are not overlooked because of too much centralization? The minister did say a few minutes ago that there were several branch research laboratories, but we should like to have further information on the plans of the government for spreading out research work across the whole dominion.
The second point has to do with the power which is to be given to the research council to set up corporations. They have not that power at the present time, but the resolution reads:
... to provide for the creation of corporations to carry out certain powers of the council which may be more conveniently performed by a separate corporation, and also to provide for the organization, administration and financing of such corporations.
Is the power to set up these corporations to rest with the research council, or with the government? A good deal of concern is felt about the present trend of the government in setting up crown companies. It is a new policy, one which was adopted during the war, as the minister said a few days ago, but it looks as though he had now acquired the habit of doing business through crown corporations. We should like to know just how the crown corporations are to be fitted into the framework of the research council. That brings up the question of the extent of the control the minister is to have over these

crown, corporations; and, more important still, what control parliament is to have over them. The danger in setting up these corporations has been that they are so far away from parliament that they might as well be in another world so far as effective control by the elected representatives of the people is concerned. They are right outside the control of the Canadian people.
Another point has to do with the type of employee. Under the present Research Council Act employees can be appointed by the governor in council-the minister will correct me if I am wrong-and I presume that that power is to be continued; in other words, this greatly enlarged staff of the research council will not be subject to the Civil Service Act or the civil service commission. Will that principle apply also to employees of the corporations set up under the research council? Are they to constitute what might be called a super-civil service? We are getting a long way from the intention of parliaments in the past, which was that the civil service should be under the Civil Service Act. What is the plan with regard to the employees of the research council and of the new corporations?
Finally will the minister explain why it is necessary to provide for the continuance of the committee of the privy council on industrial and scientific research. That seems to be amply covered in the act as it stands at the present time. Who are the members of the privy council on this committee, and what are the plans with regard to the setting up of an executive committee of the research council? The minister said nothing about that in his opening statement, and I think he should give us an explanation of the type of executive committee which it is proposed to set up under the amendments that are. to be made.

I shall be glad to give what information I have on the subjects mentioned. In the matter of conducting research outside headquarters at Ottawa, the war has already furnished developments of that kind and has proven the desirability of not concentrating all operations of the council in one locality. As my hon. friend knows, a branch of the research council is being established in the prairies and will be charged particularly with finding a solution for problems which affect the prairie provinces and which are not common to other parts of Canada. Consideration is also being given to research facilities in British Columbia. Plans are being considered for facilities on quite a substantial scale which will operate in conjunction with the university of British Columbia. Similarly, consideration is being given to the development of research facilities in the maritime provinces.
Research facilities are at present integrated with the facilities of the provinces. Close integration has been established for the purpose of preventing overlapping in the work of the two organizations, and this is now being extended into the field of private research, the object being to coordinate public research and private research to eliminate any overlap.
In the matter of crown corporations, the purpose is to separate certain operations of the council, which are themselves attaining very sizable proportions. For example, the council controls a considerable number of patents. The number was greatly increased during the war. These have a commercial value which should be exploited. It is simply a corporation to hold patents and exploit them for the crown. In the United States a corporation functions for a similar purpose in conjunction with national research facilities there. I see none of the dangers mentioned by my hon. friends in a corporation of the kind, which simply paves the way for keeping the books on the operations and bringing a balance sheet before parliament.

It has allowed us to check the pricing of the commodities. It has allowed us to watch the operations more closely than would have been the case under another form of accounting. My endeavour throughout has been to bring government transactions into corporate form, for reasons which I believe are good for operation and good for the conduct of those responsible for carrying out those operations.
Under this bill two corporations are proposed. One is definitely required at the moment, and that is a corporation to own and commercialize patents owned by the national research council. As regards the second, it has not been definitely decided, but I am of the opinion that Chalk River should be operated as a corporation.

Research Council
into the estimates in the form in which we usually get them in the various departments would give us no picture of what was being done; yet we have to safeguard the employees of this organization from political interference. subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF VICE-PRESIDENTS AND EXECUTIVE COMMITTEE, ETC.
speechtext: "rtSe minister said something about patents, and if I understood him correctly I gather it may be intended to have the national research council set up corporations to carry on manufacturing. I am glad to see the minister shake his head, indicating that it is not the intention under this bill for the national research council or the government to go into the manufacturing of anything that may be developed and patented. I always thought the research council did good work, that the country owed a great deal to what has been developed there, and in the past I was under the impression that when anything worth while was developed the patent was put up for sale and purchased by some company which would carry on the manufacture. Is that the way it is to be done?

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF VICE-PRESIDENTS AND EXECUTIVE COMMITTEE, ETC.
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF VICE-PRESIDENTS AND EXECUTIVE COMMITTEE, ETC.
speechtext:
I am glad to hear that. In the course of his remarks the minister said something about roads and also medical research. In what way is the council to cooperate with the provinces? At present all roads, with the exception of those in the far northwest, are under the control of the provinces, though perhaps in connection with the

trans-Canada highway, which is now almost completed, the government may have something to say. What would any research council in Ottawa have to do with roads? Ontario carries on its own research work in connection with road materials for the construction of provincial highways; would we not be interfering with provincial jurisdiction in that regard? I also understand that everything pertaining to medicine comes directly under the provinces. I have never heard of any federal medical college giving doctors licences to practise, so it seems to me that this .matter too comes under provincial control. Something was also said about scholarships. What can the federal government do in reference to scholarships? Is that not entirely an educational question? In the past the provinces have been very jealous of their control of all matters pertaining to education.
I do not like to take from what I have heard that it is the intention of the government to continue to operate crown companies. I had hoped the government was going to get out of -operating crown companies at the earliest possible moment, because no one can convince me that every crown company can operate with anything like the same degree of efficiency or economy as a private company. If I .were convinced that the plant set up at Haley's had been operated economically it might be an argument in favour of crown companies, but as the minister knows, this country has already put-he will know if I am wrong, and I do not know if I am right-two or perhaps three million dollars into the proposition at Haley's; that will never come back to the country. The same thing applies to the crown company at Fort McMurray, where we have already expended approximately $2,000,000. Later I am going to try to find out what is going to be done up there. The plant has been burned down, and some insurance is due to somebody. I should say the government should take that insurance, put it into the public treasury and get out of that undertaking altogether. As far as I have observed, crown companies cannot operate with the same efficiency as private companies. Why? It is as plain as a-b-c. In a private company there is incentive to develop and produce, to sit up all night and experiment, as I have done times without number, with no extra remuneration but because it was my duty to see that the company existed and went ahead. There is not that inducement in a government institution. I had hoped that instead of creating crown companies which would remain in existence at government expense, the reverse would be the policy. There is no trick whatever in operating a company if you can

Research Council
put your hand into the public treasury to meet the deficits of operation. Private companies cannot do that. The factories in your riding, Mr. Chairman, cannot do that; they have to operate on a businesslike basis.
On the other hand I am firmly in favour of the research council developing what they can and proving what they can, if they at once dispose of it to the public by tender and get out of it themselves. Then I would see some hope for development along that line; but if the government is going to operate plants I just cannot see that at all. For a while some of these plants the government has set up may have to be kept in operation by the crown, until they can be advantageously disposed of. No doubt in the end there will be losses to the country. I am not going to blame anyone for that, because many of these crown companies would not have been set up if it had not been necessary to do it for war purposes. So far as that is concerned, for whatever has been achieved I congratulate those responsible for setting up companies that private industry could not and perhaps would not set up because they did not have the money with which to do it. Now that the war is over I think it is time for the government to get out of all manufacturing, with the possible exception of military production, since there seems to be quite a strong feeling that war equipment should be produced by the government.
That is about all I have to say at this stage. I am reassured by what the minister indicated when he nodded his head a couple of times, but I should be a great deal more reassured if I knew that in due course the government would be entirely out of the manufacturing of anything.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF VICE-PRESIDENTS AND EXECUTIVE COMMITTEE, ETC.
speechtext: The national research council has been taking the lead in medical research since its inception. There has been a very strong medical committee for many years, under the direction of the council, and it is the desire of the profession that these activities should be enlarged rather than restricted. There is no difference between the provinces and the dominion as to medical research. It is a little different from anything having to do with the practice of medicine. Medical research is a valuable part of the service of the national research council. The same applies to dental research. Research into road making and road building materials is also a subject, as far as science is concerned, which is and has been of interest to the council. I know the provincial governments are also interested in research. I assume anything planned in that direction will be at least with the knowledge and approval of provincial agencies.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF VICE-PRESIDENTS AND EXECUTIVE COMMITTEE, ETC.
speechtext: Are we not going to overlap with provinces having their own research institutions? I know there is one in Toronto. The minister's proposal is that there will be research institutions under the control of this government, which will be operating in the various provinces. If there is to be one in Ontario, for instance, how will it cooperate with^the institution at Queen's Park?

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF VICE-PRESIDENTS AND EXECUTIVE COMMITTEE, ETC.
speechtext: The greatest precaution is being taken to prevent overlapping of federal government research with provincial government research. I am sure there will be no overlapping.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF VICE-PRESIDENTS AND EXECUTIVE COMMITTEE, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, while it is always comforting to see Mr. Speaker apply the rules not only against the humble private members but also against ministers of the crown, yet I must say I was sorry the minister did not have a chance to continue his explanation when he spoke upon the introduction of the resolution. I should hope that before long he would discuss any point which appeared in his original memorandum, even though he does not refer specifically to the sections involved.
Meantime I should like to know what is being done in respect of this great problem by other countries. This is not a problem singular only to Canada; rather it is one which the United States, Great Britain and other great powers must be working. Perhaps we could borrow some suggestions from them. On the other hand we may be blazing a trail along lines much better than the ones they are adopting.
Secondly I should like him to explain the relationship between the council, as it will be reconstructed, and the three national defence services. As the minister mentioned a while ago, the privy council committee on industrial and scientific research did not meet as frequently as it might have. We might assume from that the Department of National Defence was not as active in putting forth its point of view, or of having research carried on by the central council, as it might otherwise have been.
I should like him to speak briefly on the responsibilities for these various corporations envisaged by the minister, two of which I believe' are to be formed at the present time and perhaps more in the future. What is to be the form of reporting to parliament? Will the same practice be followed as is followed by the Canadian National Railways, which reports to a parliamentary committee set up from one parliament to another? OMs it to report to a select committee of some other description? In connection with the reporting by the Canadian National Rail-
Research Council

ways, I believe it is a well managed company, and one relatively free from outside influences. Yet when they appear before a parliamentary committee only for one week in a year, the background members of parliament may have acquired in the preceding year has been more or less lost in the interval.
I would welcome a proposal from the minister for a committee of parliament ifhich would have continuing interest in and supervision over the policies and general affairs of the corporations he intends to set up.
Perhaps it might be well to have an officer with functions modelled somewhat after those of the auditor general. He would be responsible to parliament, would report directly to it and not to the minister or to any agency of government. Because once the principle of private ownership and incentive is abandoned, sometimes the minute supervision so necessary to the effective carrying on of a company's operations is removed.
The matter of the relationship between federal research organizations and research laboratories, such as those mentioned by the minister as being located in the prairie provinces, British Columbia and the maritimes, has been discussed by the hon. member for Davenport. While the minister has said that every precaution has been taken to prevent overlapping, the very fear in the mind of the minister that there might be overlapping would lead one to the conclusion that certain existing research facilities could very well do the work without creating new agencies. If there is a danger of overlapping, there is the necessary implication that that which already exists is capable of doing the work. I hope the minister will be as specific as possible on this point.
Some hon. members in this section of the house are afraid that the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply, who is undoubtedly able in many respects, has a tendency to gather unto himself many threads of power which soon become strong ropes. If some of the measures giving him those powers were used to their fullest capacity we would certainly find that the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply had become the economic dictator of our country. In this instance he is setting up a research organization not only in Ottawa but in the various provinces. He must be careful not to overlap with certain existing -and, in this instance-provincial research institutions.
May I say a few words with respect to patents? I understand the minister wishes to set up these corporations in order to exploit them. I do not like the use of the word "ex-

ploitation" in connection with a publicly-owned company . I think the word has been reserved to our friends of the C.C.F. who like to use it in connection with certain other forms of enterprise. As one of their witnesses before a parliamentary committee once said, the words "exploit" and "monopoly" are emotional words, and we should be very careful how we use them. I do wish to learn from the ' minister whether any patents evolved by the research institution will be available to private industry upon payment of reasonable fees, or is it the intention to exploit them-if you like-or develop them to their utmost, and collect as much by way of fees as possible? It is not unreasonable to expect that patents thus developed should be used to recover some of the expense which has gone into research. However we find in respect of Polymer, for instance, that thal process is being used exclusively by one - company. This afternoon, when the orders of the day were called, a question was asked as to the cost of producing a pound of this synthetic rubber. We were told that this information was not available, although we appear here on behalf of our constituents, and are all shareholders and owners of the company. In explanation the minister said it would be unfair to Polymer to give the information because the effect would be to give competitors in the synthetic and natural crude rubber fields an advantage to which ordinarily they would not be entitled. I cannot see that in respect of a publicly-owned corporation such as Polymer the reason given by the minister was adequate. I hope he will give the committee further information as to the fees to be charged for these patents.
The minister said that he favoured setting up separate companies because of the process of corporation accounting, and that assets and liabilities would be apparent on company statements. I hope if these separate companies are set up, and corporation accounts are kept for them, some consideration will be given, not necessarily to the appointment of private auditors, but to having the auditor general look after the auditing of the accounts of the separate companies. The auditor general's report is looked forward to every year, and he could do this work most effectively. I hope there will be no reason to feel that accounts are not properly audited as far as income and outgo are concerned. Many of us have the suspicion-sometimes it is well founded and perhaps at other times it is just a suspicion-that when a corporation is owned by the government it receives assistance from other instrumentalities of government. The Trans-Canada Air Lines, for example, has

Research Council
virtually a monopoly of the airways of this country. The amount of revenue that T.C.A. takes in or the expenditures which it makes are not considered in relation to the appropriations made for the Department of Trans. port for the upkeep of air fields in this country. Sometimes the relationship between a government-owned corporation which publishes a balance sheet showing a profit in a particular year is so close to a government department which does not operate under balance sheet accounting that the profit and loss of the corporation is lost sight of because many things are done for the corporation by the government agency which would otherwise not have been done.

speechtext: How about the Canadian Pacific Air Lines? Does that company not use the same facilities?

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF VICE-PRESIDENTS AND EXECUTIVE COMMITTEE, ETC.
speechtext:
I said that the T.C.A. has virtually a monopoly in this country. That answers the question.
Will the government once and for all declare its policy with regard to municipal taxation? Many of our municipalities have had to carry a great burden during the war because large factories were erected and in some cases Wartime Housing carried on operations. The municipalities obtained no revenue from these operations, and yet they had to provide all municipal services, including education.
The profits and revenue of the national research council from year to year should be allowed to circulate instead of being revoted by the house, as was suggested by the previous speaker. In the case of Canadian National Railways any revenue above operations must, under the provisions of the 1937 Railways Act, go into the consolidated revenue fund. Then if parliament in its wisdom sees fit to vote money for capital expenditures, that is done by this house. Unless some adequate explanation is offered, I believe that the same method should be adopted in connection with the research council.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF VICE-PRESIDENTS AND EXECUTIVE COMMITTEE, ETC.
speechtext:
My hon. friend has touched upon many subjects, and I shall be glad to answer those that I can remember. He suggested that the accounts of the company should be audited by the auditor general or someone appointed by him. That has been taken care of already. The accounts of all crown companies are audited by the auditor general, and the public accounts give the detailed balance sheet of each crown company operation. The comments of the auditor general also apply to the conduct of crown companies. A similar provision is contained in the Research Council Act, and this would
apply to any crown company organized by the council. It would be subject to audit by the auditor general and the details of its operations would be published in the public accounts. Any provision that parliament may wish to make for the examination of the annual report of the national research counci' is a matter for parliament.
I would suggest that the accounts of all crown companies might very well be submitted to a parliamentary committee, perhaps the committee on railways and shipping, government owned. The scope of that committee might be enlarged so that it could undertake the examination of all crown companies. That is my suggestion, but it is a matter for parliament to decide. My hon. friend is as free to move that the report of the national research council be handled in that way as is any member of the government.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF VICE-PRESIDENTS AND EXECUTIVE COMMITTEE, ETC.
speechtext: That committee sits but one week in the year, which means that fifty-one weeks intervene between each sitting. That makes it difficult to have any continuity. It is the responsibility of the minister to decide matters of policy. Can he suggest any way in which there would be continuity in examination of the operations of these companies?

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF VICE-PRESIDENTS AND EXECUTIVE COMMITTEE, ETC.
speechtext: The auditor general exercises supervision, and the comptroller of the treasury keeps a careful check on accounts.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF VICE-PRESIDENTS AND EXECUTIVE COMMITTEE, ETC.
speechtext: What'about policy?

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF VICE-PRESIDENTS AND EXECUTIVE COMMITTEE, ETC.
speechtext: I suppose policy is the responsibility of the minister under whose jurisdiction the various companies operate.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF VICE-PRESIDENTS AND EXECUTIVE COMMITTEE, ETC.
speechtext: The minister told us where the different branches of the research council were to be located, and I was surprised to hear that no provision had been made to operate a branch of the council in conjunction with the university of Toronto, which is located in perhaps the largest industrial centre in Canada. Why was that decision arrived at, and why are some of their buildings not to be' used? What coordination is there between the Ontario research foundation and the national research council? On the surface it would appear that much of the expense of research work is to fall upon the shoulders of the university of Toronto.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF VICE-PRESIDENTS AND EXECUTIVE COMMITTEE, ETC.
speechtext:
The university of Toronto has been closely associated with the national research council, especially during the war years. Some very substantial items of research have been carried out, and carried out successfully. I believe the amount of work that the university will carry out, for the council will be limited by its capacity to handle it.
Research Council

The council will be very glad to send the university any items of research which the latter feels it can carry out along with its own major activities.
The council has worked closely with all universities, and has encouraged them to take on research work organized by the national council. I think that will continue to be the policy of the national research council. So far as the research foundation of Ontario is concerned, it is my recollection that the director of the foundation is a member of the national research council. In any event he works closely with the chairman of the national research council. I do not think my hon. friend need have any fear that the work of the two organizations is not closely coordinated.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF VICE-PRESIDENTS AND EXECUTIVE COMMITTEE, ETC.
speechtext: The minister said that the university of Toronto would carry on research work and that the research council would give it as much research as it could handle. I am not a graduate of the university of Toronto; I went to McGill, but the university of Toronto is a great university and has a very large student body, which at the present time are very much cramped for quarters. The minister has said that plans have been made for buildings in connection with the university of British Columbia and, I suppose, in connection with the university of Manitoba and the university of British Columbia. If new buildings are to be built in connection with these other universities the university of Toronto should receive consideration because it is a great research centre located in a large industrial centre and urgently requires additional accommodation. Some time ago hon. members brought before the house the situation in connection with Research Enterprises. I presume that those buildings are sold. At all events it does seem to me that since new buildings are to be built in connection with other universities something should be done to provide more premises for the university of Toronto.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF VICE-PRESIDENTS AND EXECUTIVE COMMITTEE, ETC.
speechtext: The national research council erects buildings for itself and not for universities, but it happens that some buildings it erects for itself are, for purposes of administration, located adjacent to universities. If my hon. friend will visit the important annex to the university of Toronto known as Ajax he will find magnificent buildings there housing a large student body. No. 10 on to-day's order paper is to provide for the operation and financing of government companies. Would the minister explain to us the relationship between the corporations to be set up under the research council and the companies contemplated in order No. 10?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF VICE-PRESIDENTS AND EXECUTIVE COMMITTEE, ETC.
speechtext: I do not think it is competent for the committee to discuss order No. 10 while on this resolution.

speechtext: Perhaps, Mr. Chairman, I might be allowed to say that order No. 10 makes provision for all crown companies, and that the resolution now before us provides for the research council supervising the activities of certain crown companies.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF VICE-PRESIDENTS AND EXECUTIVE COMMITTEE, ETC.
speechtext:
Therefore the crown companies contemplated under the resolution now under discussion will be governed by the measure contemplated under order No. 10. The minister has mentioned th^,t he proposes to establish two companies, one for the owning and commercializing of patents, another for the Polymer Corporation, and I think he mentioned a third, for the Eldorado company. The resolution before us is to give the research council power to create and operate as many crown companies as it deems desirable. I am therefore confused by the answer given by the minister to the hon. member for Davenport that it was not proposed that the crown companies set up under this resolution would be operating companies, because most certainly Eldorado and Polymer are operating companies.
Before this resolution passes we should have a statement by the minister defining the limits of the power of the research council to create crown companies and to operate crown companies in a commercial way because, as the resolution reads, it gives almost unlimited power to the research council to establish crown corporations for any and every purpose that they could possibly conceive of as having anything to do with research.
We realize, of course, that research is one of the most important things that the House of Commons could discuss in these reconstruction days, and I think every member is zealous to see to it that Canada maintains and enlarges her research activities carried on during the war so that they can apply to peace-time industry. But we should be very careful to ensure that the research council confines its activities to research for the public benefit. I should not like to see a crown corporation set up and' removed entirely from the control of parliament as some of the crown companies now are. I should not like to see any crown company established and put in a position

Research Council
where we would have to question any one of three or more ministers about its activities as we have to do in connection with the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. I would not want it to be thought that because the crown companies will produce an annual balance sheet the House of Commons will get much more information about them than if the information were contained in the auditor general's report, because that has not been the experience of the house. The fact that a financial statement of a crown company appears in the auditor general's report or in public accounts and that the statement is audited and supervised by the comptroller of the treasury or by the auditor general does not of necessity give parliament the particulars it desires of the operations of the company. I think we all will agree in this day of reconstruction that the government in carrying out the mandate of the people of Canada and administering affairs of the scope of the national research council's work should do so not behind closed doors, not in secret, not in a manner that will withhold information from competitors in private enterprise or even from other nations, but should act for the benefit of mankind and for the information of private enterprise.
The Minister of Reconstruction gave some reasons this afternoon why he thought that the cost per pound of manufacturing rubber in Polymer should not be given to the public, but the reasons did not impress many of us. Polymer operated during the war in a time of emergency for the benefit of the people of Canada, and if it is to continue in time of peace it must be prepared to show that it can operate economically and must convince its shareholders, the people of Canada, that it is a wise and prudent investment for them to continue. But we cannot get that information if the particulars are withheld from us, nor can private industry benefit by the research work done at Polymer if its research information is not to be made public. It is but the part of prudence for any man before deciding whether an enterprise is sound or not to be able to compare its efficiency in production with that of its competitors. I therefore trust that the minister will make a statement defining the scope of the power that is to be given to the national research council to create and operate crown companies. Such a statement would allay the fears of many of us and probably expedite the passage of this resolution, because then we would be in a better position to judge what course we should take.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF VICE-PRESIDENTS AND EXECUTIVE COMMITTEE, ETC.
speechtext: The purpose of the national research council is to promote research, and incidentally to the promotion of research it finds itself involved in certain business activities *which it is not primarily organized to handle. For example, sixty per cent of the time of the chairman of the national research council is given to problems both of organization and of business. The purpose of the reorganization of the national research council staff is to provide assistance to the chairman, who is also director of research, and relieve him of certain business activities by placing them in the hands of corporations. As I have said, the handling of patents involves a great deal of time, and in my opinion the organization for handling patents at the moment is not adequate. I believe that a corporation which will relieve the national research council of that duty is desirable. Whether a corporation proves to be the best means of handling Chalk River I am not at the moment prepared to say, but at present it is the view of those associated with the project that it can be handled to best advantage through a corporation. Chalk River involves the administration of an industrial plant, a townsite, the purchase of raw materials and the sale of the product. It has business activities as well as research activities, and it may very well be that the scientists there would prefer to have the business administration of Chalk River handled by a corporation so that they would be free to devote all their time to science.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF VICE-PRESIDENTS AND EXECUTIVE COMMITTEE, ETC.
speechtext: Is it run by the research council now?

speechtext:
No. At the moment it is
being operated by the contractors who built the project. It will be turned over to the national research council when it has been thoroughly tested and can be regarded as a fully operating project.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF VICE-PRESIDENTS AND EXECUTIVE COMMITTEE, ETC.
speechtext:
Will the minister make a statement regarding his intentions in the
Research Council

matter of limiting the scope under which any companies which may be created under this measure will operate. The purpose of crown corporations is to publish a financial statement once every year. That is done through the annual report which is published in the public accounts of Canada. I hope we shall not hear too much about my not being prepared to give the cost of producing rubber at Sarnia last month.

speechtext: One object of the legislation is to appoint a vice-president of the council who will be a business man in charge of business administration. At the moment we are trying to correct that weakness in seeking the power to form companies. I am not putting a limitation on that.

speechtext:
The hon. member for Carleton asked a question and I am not sure whether the minister answered it clearly. I understood the hon. member to ask whether

the information obtained as a result of researches carried out by the national research council would be made public or be given to private enterprise. My understanding is that such information will be made public in connection with the development of any process after it has been proved successful. I believe the minister indicated that at the end of the year, in their annual report, information on these various researches will be made public. Is that so?	.

speechtext: Steps are being taken for a wide dissemination of the results of research. I have told the house on a previous occasion that the Department of Reconstruction and Supply has a particular branch devoted to making the results of research immediately available to industry, and the national research council is made acquainted with the requirements of industry in the direction of research. In every province a representative of the department will consider any problems of research that may be helpful to the economy of that province. Further, the research council will make its library available to industry or to any user of scientific information, and if necessary, it will initiate research to supply any deficiency in available information. The latter would probably be at the expense of a business firm which might require the information. However, discoveries of the national research council are patented and it is now the practice to patent all discoveries of reasonable value. Many are in use and many patent holders already pay fees to the council for the use of the patents. Hon. members will agree that anyone wishing to use a patent of the national research council should pay its full market value, and it is to obtain the revenue that should properly come from the patents of the council that the proposed corporation to handle patents is to be established.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF VICE-PRESIDENTS AND EXECUTIVE COMMITTEE, ETC.
speechtext: Will it be possible for any private enterprise to acquire a patent from the research council and then, as has often been suggested is the practice of some establishment-whether it is true I am not in a position to say-to hang the patent on the wall and simply keep it there? speechtext:
So far, our discussion
seems to have been directed along industrial lines. The national research council seems to be endeavouring to broaden the field. In listening to the minister I heard him speak of research in the medical field. That is admirable, but we should extend our research effort into the economic field. At this point may I congratulate the hon. member for Lethbridge on the recommendations he made for research into the proper distribution of goods. What efforts will be made toward research in the medical field? I mention that because, like many other hon. members, I *have received many letters about the terrible disease of arthritis. There does not seem to be any material progress made in that field. Then there is cancer, which has been brought before the house on other occasions, especially by the late member for Portage la Prairie, who was especially interested in that subject, and took an active part in the discussion. This is one field in which the research council could do important work. It could assist in other ways. It could assist in research into the control and elimination of not only cancer but also arthritis. It is all very well to speak of the economic standard of our people, but if the national health is deteriorating, then the national economy will also deteriorate. Efforts should be made by the research council to extend their studies into the medical field to, see what can be done with these two diseases, cancer and arthritis. Is any progress being made along that line?

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF VICE-PRESIDENTS AND EXECUTIVE COMMITTEE, ETC.
speechtext:
The direction of medical
research is in the hands of a committee of the national research council. on which the medical societies of Canada have representation. I cannot say what work is being conducted in the two particular fields mentioned. Of course, many millions of dollars are being spent at the present time in many countries on cancer research. Certain research is being carried on here, but I cannot say to what extent. All the scientific information in that field is pooled and we sincerely hope that a cure can be found for cancer, which is the greatest killer of all diseases. However, the medical councils of the country decide the lines of activity which will be followed in medical research. The purpose is to make the funds available to the council go as far as possible, and to undertake lines of research which will be most helpful to the Canadian public.

Does the national

speechtext: Yes. Our national research council maintains in Washington an office with a considerable personnel for that specific purpose. It also has an office and staff in London, England. It has facilities for obtaining the results of discoveries in any part of the world.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF VICE-PRESIDENTS AND EXECUTIVE COMMITTEE, ETC.
speechtext:
This afternoon a good deal has been said about the Polymer Corporation. I should like to remind the committee that after Pearl Harbor, when our supply of natural rubber disappeared, the firms which normally might be expected to manufacture rubber were not particularly interested in risking any of their capital. Had not the minister in his wisdom been prepared to invest $50 million of Canadian money in this project, the war might not have ended as soon as it did. Now that it has been demonstrated that a high quality of synthetic rubber can be made by Polymer, there are those who think the government should retire from this field. The minister would be wise not to pay too much attention to those who argue that the free enterprisers should have clear sailing in this field in which the people have invested $50 million. I believe it has been demonstrated that the quality of the rubber compares favourably with rubber made anywhere
Research Council

on the continent. The facilities there are adequate to make all we need here and some for export. Should we now at this stage decide that there should be five, six, seven or a dozen similar plants in the country, or shall we continue to use the facilities that are there? Hon. members to my right can be assured that the operation of this corporation will be reviewed by the people's representatives in this parliament from time to time, just as the operations of the Canadian National Railways, and the Trans-Canada Air Lines are reviewed from time to time by the people's representatives, and that a satisfactory explanation can be given for the operation. Even the most ardent supporters of the Canadian Pacific Railway company cannot make a very good case against the publicly-owned railways. *
Earlier this afternoon the minister said that it would be a splendid thing to have men working in research work move freely from university to research council, from research council into private enterprise, or back into universities. I do not share this view. A research problem is something a man cannot pick up and handle in a short time. There are men who are working on one problem for a lifetime. Those who are in the national research council should be placed in a position so that they might continue in the government service for their lifetime if there were a chance of making a decent livelihood. It is a pity that they should be obliged to leave the national research council or any public organization to go to private enterprise at a time when they are bringing up a family and are not receiving enough to make ends meet. We have had a number of distinguished scientists attached to the national research 

council who have been working, certainly during the war years, on compensation entirely out of line with the service they perform. It is extremely difficult to estimate in dollars and cents what some of this research has meant. I understand that at the national research council glycol has been made from low grade wheat. It has been used in cars as anti-freeze and compares favourably with Prestone. I see no reason why, when the people have spent so much money in developing a process of this kind, we should not go on and develop it, sell it to our people and find a market for our low grade wheat, and at the same time provide our car drivers with a suitable anti-freeze at a lower price than we normally pay for Prestone.
I am very glad to hear that additional money is to be spent in western Canada. I am sure the people of Saskatchewan will be pleased to learn that Doctor Larmour has been selected to direct the activities of the

research council in that province. He is one of our own graduates, a man who enjoys the confidence and respect of scientists across the country, and I am sure he will do a very good job. I am heartily in favour of research on the ground, as it were, when we have so many products going to waste. I consider it quite conceivable that during our lifetime, for instance, we may find some use for the wheat straw that is destroyed in such large quantities every year. I think it is not too much to expect that if the federal government will spend a little money in the initial stages they may do research work that will pay attractive dividends from a long-term point of view.
I should like the minister to reconsider the matter which was raised earlier, of having the employees of the national research council move freely back and forth from the university to the council, where they will get their training, and then to privately owned organizations, which will obtain the benefit of the research that has been carried on. I do not think these men should be encouraged to leave for salary reasons. I see no reason why the taxpayers cannot pay salaries as attractive as those paid by private organizations. Therefore, in formulating his plans for the future I should like the minister to make upward revisions in the salaries paid to the scientists of the research council, so that none of these men will feel obliged to leave for financial reasons.

speechtext:
I was pleased to hear the minister say that it was the intention to decentralize the work of the national research council. If that principle could be applied also to manufacturing in this country it would be a great benefit to all. The minister said that a research branch would be set up in the maritime provinces. I should like to ask at what point he contemplates setting up this branch and what particular work it is proposed to do. At the present time, for instance, we have a fish experimental station at St. Andrews. I should like to know whether the work of the council would be correlated-with the work of the fisheries departments, both dominion and provincial.
In connection with the method of disposing of these patents, I understand they are not sold outright to any particular company but are given to the companies for the development of certain articles. Would different companies be allowed to bid for the patent, or would the council itself decide what particular company should obtain a certain patent? Then, if that company did not deal with it satisfactorily, could the council exercise its authority at a later time and take away from

Research Council
any particular company a patent which the council felt had not been developed to the fullest possible extent? These are questions the minister might answer, if he will.

speechtext: I have one other question somewhat along the same line which the minister might answer when he is replying to the last speaker. I was wondering what research work the council does on behalf of other governmental bodies in Canada, that is, municipal and provincial governments. The provincial governments have control of our natural resources, and a vast amount of research work could be done in connection with the best uses to be made of those resources. Does the national research council do this work for the provinces, and what are the financial arrangements as between the dominion and the various municipal or provincial governments?

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF VICE-PRESIDENTS AND EXECUTIVE COMMITTEE, ETC.
speechtext:
As far as research facilities in the maritime provinces are concerned, I simply said that they were being contemplated. I doubt if the study of the matter has reached the point where we can determine the exact location or the exact nature of the work. However, the work will be supplementary and additional to the work at present being carried on. In any event there is nothing in this resolution dealing with that particular enterprise, and I am not at the moment prepared to be any more definite than that. Feld representatives of the branch are operating in the maritime provinces, in association with the. Department of Reconstruction and Supply.	.
The policy in connection with the use of patents is determined by the national research council, and in future will be determined by the council operating through the proposed corporations. I assume the policies would vary, having regard to the nature of the patents and the use to which they were to be put. For example, perhaps the most valuable patent owned by the council, at least the one I know most about, is concerned with turning ammonia nitrate into prills. When ammonia nitrate was first put on the market as fertilizer by Canada it was referred to in the southern states as tombstone fertilizer. It was found because of moisture, that if a bag were left out in the open for two or three weeks it would turn into a pillar of concrete. Employees of the government working at Calgary discovered a way to turn this material into small pellets known as prills, and by manufacturing fertilizer in that way we have found a method of marketing our surplus ammonia in a satisfactory form. That patent is owned by the national research 63260-120
council. We have applications from almost every country making ammonia for the use of the patent, and a policy is being studied in that connection.

speechtext: What was the annual salary of the young fellow who discovered that process?

speechtext: He was one of our more expensive men. I should like to make it clear that in referring to a turnover of scientists it was not my purpose to suggest that the national research council should starve them out. I have always encouraged young engineers who have been associated with me to try somebody else after a time, to broaden their experience. I think it is a good thing for scientists to move from laboratory to laboratory and in that way build up their background.

speechtext: That is what we recommend to the people of Canada.

The hon. member for Melfort asked a question in regard to financial arrangements as between provincial and federal governments. Matters of science are treated as matters of interest to all the people. I do not think there is any exchange of funds as between the federal government and the provincial governments, unless in connection with a problem in which both are interested, but which is assigned to one, along with a financial grant. I believe the national research council would be prepared to undertake any problem it thought was of importance to any part of Canada. For example, research into the use of wheat for glycol is being carried on by the national research council as one

Research Council

of its projects, and I presume that would be one of the projects transferred to the laboratory in Saskatchewan for further development.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF VICE-PRESIDENTS AND EXECUTIVE COMMITTEE, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I had not thought that Nos. 10 and 14 on the order paper would interlock to such a great extent. What I shall have to say will refer more particularly to No. 10, and I shall say it at a later time.
The point which now concerns me has to do with research chemists, as it applies to Polymer, and also as it may apply to many other corporations. We know that in the development of Polymer time was a big factor, and that both governments obtained the support of engineers and chemists not only from the United States and Canada but from Europe.
What concerns me now is that in the area of Sarnia, where Polymer is located, there is a tendency on the part of many of these chemists, some of whom were employed by the Imperial Oil company, to terminate their contracts with Polymer. I am advised that some of the top men in Polymer who were most instrumental in the production of rubber so quickly, when time was an important factor, have the option of returning to Imperial Oil within a year, and that by doing so they will be eligible to take' advantage of the retirement and pension schemes offered by that company.
I know, and I have no doubt the minister knows, that inducements are being offered to the head chemists at Polymer by private industry. I hope that in order to preserve this important industry the minister will see to it that we retain our top chemists, scientific research men and engineers. After all is said and done, we know what private industry will pay men of a high calibre. In this connection, one might compare what is paid to the head chemist of Imperial Oil with the amount paid to the head chemist at Polymer. If Polymer wishes to have men equal in ability to those employed by the private company, an inducement by way of price must be held out. We are alarmed at the fact that many of these men will be leaving, although they still have eleven months to serve. However, this fact leads us to doubt the permanency of the plant, and we want assurance that the head chemists will be retained.
I am not so much concerned about the question which seemed to bother some hon. members this afternoon. A week ago last Tuesday the minister gave the price of rubber, and also the price of it last September and October. I notice there has been very little change. I also notice that some of his employees in the Polymer Corporation have

given out prices of rubber from time to time. I do not see how it can be any great secret. I am not quarreling about the minister's not answering the question because, after all is said and done, some of this information can be obtained later. A week ago last Tuesday the minister told us that the price was 204 cents; and why he had to reject the question to-day, I do not know.

speechtext: The question was as to the cost of producing rubber. I am willing at any time to publish from the roof tops the selling price of rubber. But the question asked was as to the cost of producing rubber last month. While I may be willing to tell the house that last month was the best month we ever had, so far as costs are concerned, yet I am not anxious to tell the world what it costs us from month to month to produce rubber at Sarnia.

speechtext: I did not ask it from month to month.

speechtext:
I think the hon. member did, as a matter of fact. This is the question:
1.	What is the present cost per pound for the production of the different types of rubber produced by the Polymer Corporation Limited?
The present cost would be the cost per month. Then he asked:
2.	What was the cost of the production of the different types of rubber by the Polymer Corporation Limited during each quarter for the year ending March 31, 1945-March 31, 1946?
We are attempting to hold our research staff at Polymer. We need that staff, to keep up to date. Through the research work carried on at Polymer we have substantially improved the quality of our rubber.
The St. Clair Processing Company Limited had on loan from Imperial Oil certain chemists involved in plant operation. Now that the St. Clair Processing Company Limited is no longer in charge of operations at Polymer, some of those chemists are returning to Imperial Oil. Polymer has a permanent staff of chemists. The head chemist came to us from the oil industry. He left that industry to come to us, and I have heard nothing to indicate that he intends to leave us to return to that industry, at least in the near future.
We were admitted to the patent pool, which controls all the rubber patents, on the undertaking that Polymer would spend a certain amount of money each year on research work, and that the results from such research would be turned into the pool. We are carrying out that obligation. We believe that our contributions to the pool of information respecting synthetic rubber are well up to the expectations of those who admitted us to the pool.

speechtext: I have several questions to ask, and I am prepared to submit them separately or in a group.

speechtext: Could the minister say a word as to the extent to which an expansion of research work is contemplated, provided that the bill goes into effect? We all know that many scientists have drifted to the United States, and one of the chief reasons given for this is that the salary inducement in Canada is not adequate to keep them here. This is a matter of great concern to us all.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF VICE-PRESIDENTS AND EXECUTIVE COMMITTEE, ETC.
speechtext:
As I said, prior to the war the personnel of the national research council numbered 300; it is now about 2,000. The purpose of this bill is to expand the structure of the council in order to permit it to administer the number of scientists who are at present under its' control. We are adding vice-presidents and enlarging the administrative staff at the top. With regard to salaries, as my hon. fridnd knows a royal commission is now investigating higher salaries in the public service, and the civil service commission is considering a new scale of salaries for the national research council. I hope that we can improve the salary position of our scientists so that it will be comparable at least with that in other countries which are competing with us for scientists.
However, there is an acute shortage of scientists throughout this continent and abroad. I suppose the atomic energy development has in a measure been responsible for this, but the fact remains that any man of science can step out into industry to-day and double or treble his salary. I say that without fear of contradiction. I know of tremendous
Research Council

salaries being offered to men who are working here in Canada. These offers are sometimes made by Canadian industry and sometimes, perhaps more often, by industry abroad. That is the situation, and until we can develop more good scientists it will be difficult for the national research council to hold its personnel.

225. The council caused an addition to be constructed to the medical laboratory of Queen's university. The addition is currently regarded as a public work of Canada. The contract, dated October 25, 1944, with Doran Construction Company, Limited, was executed on behalf of the council by Professor G. B. Reed of the university. The plans and specifications were prepared by the Department of National Defence. The contract is on a cost-plus-a-fee basis.

The bureau of mines collected $1,481.93 for assays and analyses . . .
It then goes on to state:
Scales of fees exist, but most of the work is done without charge. The bureau's chemical laboratories performed 24,524 determinations, 1,566 gold assays and 294 silver assays in the year. These include tests made for other divisions. The scales of fees for such tests range from $2 to $7. Had all been assessed even the minimum - rate, the revenue would have been $52,768. speechtext: As I said earlier in the day, we are all entirely in favour of the continuation and extension of the work of the national research council.
