It has never been the practice of the national research council to go into
	.
the manufacturing business. For example, even during the war, all scientific discoveries in the field of radar made by the council were developed commercially elsewhere. At that time the work of the council stopped in making one prototype. A new radar device would be invented by the research council, and a prototype made, which would then be sent to Research Enterprises for manufacture, the actual manufacturing details being worked out by the crown company which was not associated with the national research council.
The present policy would be for the national research council to make the prototype. It would then be sent to a private industry, which would work out the manufacturing details and put the device on the market, or manufacture it for the armed services, as the case might be. This will continue to be the policy so far as this government is concerned. It has been decided as a matter of policy that the work formerly performed by Research Enterprises Limited will now be done by private interests. In other words, with the liquidation of Research Enterprises, it is not proposed, in future, to perform through crown companies the work which was formerly done by Research Enterprises.
The crown companies supervised by the research council will be those which will deal with the business side of the national research council. For example, in my opinion, the marketing of patents must necessarily be associated with the national research council. Further, experiments on atomic energy must, of necessity be a part of the work of the research council, and so large a part of the staff connected with that project should logically be associated with the council. If Chalk River is associated with the council, Eldorado, which furnishes the raw material for Chalk River, should also possibly be associated with the council. It has not, however, been decided finally whether Chalk River and Eldorado will be associated with the national research council. These, together with the parent corporation, are the crown companies which are envisaged at the moment. There may be one as the minimum; there may be three as the maximum. speechtext:
The house resumed from Tuesday, May 14, consideration in committee of the following resolution-Mr. Howe-Mr. Macdonald (Brantford City) in the chair:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide for the operation and financing of government companies, to define their status as agents to His Majesty, and to provide further for the superannuation, pension or other rights of the employees of such companies.

subtopic: OPERATIONS AND FINANCING-SUPERANNUATION AND PENSION PROVISIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
In a brief statement this afternoon I mentioned that I was primarily concerned with the Polymer Corporation, which is one of the companies affected by this particular resolution. Since the Polymer Corporation happens to be in my riding I should like to make some comments on this resolution. First of all, I wish to say that I appreciate the fact that this particular industry is located at the particular place where it is, which, after all, is the logical place for its location. As everyone knows, this plant is on the great lakes, and is next door to the Imperial Oil refinery. While Imperial Oil happen to be the largest refiners in the British empire, they have several refineries in Canada, and the largest in this country is at Sarnia. So that obviously this was the natural and logical place for the Polymer Corporation.
I think I should say in the beginning that we all appreciate the fact that after Pearl Harbor it became absolutely necessary that we manufacture rubber immediately. Time was of the utmost importance; cost was not. We were in a state of emergency; we were all concerned with producing rubber in order to prosecute the war successfully, and producing rubber as quickly as we could. With that in mind, this country and the United States, with support received from other scientific sources, were able to gather together a very considerable group of scientists, research engineers and chemists who pooled their knowledge to bring about the manufacture of rubber in this country. At that time we in Canada had the support of some of the most capable men in our industrial life. On the board of directors when the Polymer Corpora-

tion was incorporated we had men such as Mr. Campbell, president of the Ford Motor company, the president of Goodyear Tire, and other men of high reputation who, working with that body of scientists, were able to get together and perform a miracle. I have no hesitation in telling this committee now that, as a result, Canada was in the lead in the development of synthetic rubber, something of which we may all be proud.
I am speaking as the member for that riding. As a matter of fact this plant is located in the township in which I live. As a crown corporation it is not liable to taxation, which of course is also the case in other ridings in which crown corporations are located.
Another aspect of the question, with which I should like to deal a little later, is the security of the men who carry their dinner buckets, who are vitally interested in whether or not the present operation is continued.
I wish to deal first with the matter of taxation. The minister stated that some $50 million had been invested in this corporation. I do not attempt to suggest that if this were a private corporation that entire amount would be subject to taxation. We all know that, while land and buildings would be liable to taxation, under our assessment act the municipal assessment or taxation would be on but a small part of that total. According to the company's statement as of March 31, 1944. I find that the capital for land and buildings was in the neighbourhood of $7,000,000, in round figures, while the capital as of March 31, 1945, was about $1,250,000 more. I submit that the municipality in which this corporation is located is subjected to expense by necessity, for instance in connection with the maintenance of roads, hospitalization, administration, education and so on. I should like to give some rough figures with respect to education, having in mind the fact that, according to the minister, this corporation turned in to the government profits of some $10,000,000, apparently since the 1944 statement was issued, because in that statement we were told that the loss of the corporation was around $440,000. We find that in the six months since November 1 of the last year the cost of hospitalization was about four times the cost three years ago, and we must anticipate increased costs in that connection, though we 63260-121

do not know how great the increase will be. The same argument will apply in connection with relief.
At the time the plant was in the course of construction I happened to be on the township council, and we received from the corporation a grant of $6,000 toward the cost of road maintenance. As hon. members know, construction was carried on both winter and summer. We are not quarreling over the additional cost incurred, because time was of the utmost importance, and everyone wanted the work done in a hurry. We all know it could have been done more cheaply in peace time, and it could have been done more cheaply in the summer time, but no one objected to the work going on summer and winter because the plant had to be completed in record time, and it was. But in order to carry on that work they had to haul gravel over the roads at periods when full loads were not permitted, and as a result they gave the township $6,000 toward road maintenance. That summer they also contributed $5,000 to the general township fund, and similar annual grants have been made since that time. There was some argument as to what should be the proper amount. We did not know what the expenses would be to which I referred a moment ago, or what the increase would be.
I maintain that if this crown company is to remain a crown company and operate as such the municipality should receive some consideration by way of compensation for the additional expense incurred, which I have somewhat laboriously pointed out. I am certain that if it were a private company and were assessed as such, the assessment of that plant alone would just about equal the present assessment in the township. I am also equally confident that if it were a private company, and if it were to be assessed at a lower value, as other industries are, our revenue from Polymer would be at least $70,000 a year. If it is considered advisable to have this measure pass, some consideration should be given to these modest claims by way of compensation for the township.
I notice from the resolution that the minister has included provision "for the superannuation, pension or other rights of the employees of such companies." I should like to emphasize at this time why in my view each of these companies, in the interests of good reasoning, should be incorporated separately.	[DOT]

In the next paragraph he says:

As I said a minute ago, the minister did state as reported at page 1561, that Polymer Corporation was built at a cost of about $50 million. He said on the same day that the cost per pound of rubber was about 20J cents.

. What worries me as a businessman when I look at these figures is how I' can arrive at some intelligent answer without having a great deal more information. I have had some experience in business and I should like to have more details of these items which cover very large amounts of money. I am wondering whether certain items should be charged to profit. If so, it will alter the statement on profits and affect- the cost of rubber per pound.
Certain features in connection with this Polymer Corporation seem a little cloudy to a businessman, and any remarks I make in this connection are not intended t-o cast any reflection on anyone. As I understand it, by agreeing to this bill we shall be endorsing what has been done. I should like to quote from sessional paper 250, which sets out the operating contract between Polymer Corporation Limited and Dow Chemical of Canada Limited, dated as of May 1, 1942, but not executed until June 28, 1943, covering the operation of the styrene unit; and operating contract between Polymer Corporation Limited and Canadian Synthetic Rubber Limited, dated as of March 26, 1942, but not executed until March 22, 1944, covering the operation of the buna A copolymer plant. The note which follows is, I think, very important. It reads:
No operating contract or letter in lieu of contract relating to operation of the units being operated by St. Clair Processing Corporation Limited exists. Imperial Oil Limited and St. Clair Processing Corporation Limited have proceeded on the strength of the assurances received from the senior officials of Polymer Corporation Limited that they would be paid on a reasonable basis for services rendered and products supplied. Negotiations are proceeding.
Here we have the government or some agency of the government doing business in millions for a year or two with nothing in writing. Apparently these transactions were carried out on the strength of assurances by senior officials of the Polymer Corporation Limited. I assume that they would be the directors and Mr. Nicholson, the general manager, in whom everyone has complete confidence. I have heard it whispered here and there that Mr. Nicholson's salary of $25,000 is too large, but I want to go on record right now as saying that I happen to know Mr. Nicholson and that if the general manager of Polymer corporation is not worth $25,000 a year, he would not be the manager. After he pays his income tax he has only about one-half 6326(^-1211
of that left. However, this sort of thing, contracts on assurances, does not look like good business to a businessman.
There is no question in my mind about the future operations and1 the continued success of the Polymer corporation, but the taxpayers and the employees there are wondering just what permanency there may be. As I said this afternoon, we have had the benefit of much expert advice but, now that the war is over, these people will be returning to their own places of business, having performed their duties more or less from a patriotic point of view and having received no money therefor. Now that they have left, the government must depend upon what remains in the way of expert technical advice. The people are wondering if a change in government policy is likely to affect the jobs of these 1,800 persons, with their families, as well as their investments, the municipal obligations they have undertaken, public services and schools and that sort of thing. Are they to continue as employees? They say that rubber may be used as a means of barter between Canada and some other country and that perhaps the production of rubber, by government policy, will decrease 50 per cent. Some maintain that under private ownership, with so much invested and so many stockholders interested, they would naturally carry on to the best of their ability. We know that this government in the operation of this plant did import products duty and excise free, but that is only a matter of bookkeeping anyway. We realize that, whether it is under public ownership or private ownership, we shall have Jo compete, there being no duty on rubber, with foreign markets. We know that we have an export market in the Scandinavian countries, a bit of a market in England and a bit in the South American countries.
The point I wish to emphasize is that some of the employees who have been with this corporation a long time, some of them during the course of its construction, are sceptical, many of them, about the efficiency of government operation. They wonder what this $10 million profit means or if it is a $10 million profit. They know, for instance, that in the course of construction of Polymer there were some thirty-five or thirty-eight bunkhouses, staff houses, hospitals and so on and that some of their friends bought some of these staff houses, which cost from $25,000 to $30,000, for one or two thousand dollars as the case may be. They know also that their friends wrecked these buildings, dismantled them. I know that in one case the purchaser obtained the property for the purpose of obtaining a

The point which I think is most important to these men who have seen the scrap collectors go in with their trucks and take out scrap which was not scrap is that they wonder if that is the way the government is going to carry on this proposition.

I should like to have the position clear. I emphasized at the start, purposely, that there were certain questions I had in mind. I want to determine whether certain figures are to be considered as capital cost or to be charged against profits. We have had the statement that $10 million was made; we also had the financial statement up to March 31, 1945, giving us in some detail, very limited, capital costs; and my point is simply this, that in order to determine whether they are capital costs or must be charged against profits we must have more information. I submit, then, that I am entitled to ask the minister or the government what particular capital account or figure these amounts can be charged up to. So that we may agree on this, take the figure I have just quoted, which was $325, and the item was sold for $1.34. My argument Is that if the capital costs are as outlined by the statement, at $50 million, this represents a loss of $323.66 which must be charged up against capital, or it must be charged against profits, or it must be the amount representing the loss that would be actually sustained if you and I were operating that company. That is clear. I do not wish to be overbearing on this sort of thing. I am an Irishman; I am rather new here, and I am willing to learn.
Another item amounts to $218,058.55. That was sold for $3,500. There is another item of $286,460 which was sold for $19,000; another item of $22,350.84 which was sold for $3,650; another item of $21,076 which was sold for $1,900; and another item of $46,658.96 which was sold for $1,560. Another item of $107,597.47 was sold for $1,188.25, or T7 per cent of the cost. Another item of $269,489.13 was sold for approximately $6,000', or 2-2 per cent of the cost. The total of these eight items is $775,815.95. These items were sold for $35,602.59, or 4-5 per cent of their cost. Was that part of the capital cost of Polymer? Looking at the statement, and trying to interpret it as a businessman, one must come to the conclusion that there is a loss of $742,413.36 somewhere.
I appreciate the difference between something used and something new. I do not expect that the government through any of its agencies will realize as much on the cost if the article has been used as they would if if were new. Let us take bunk and staff houses as an example. No one expects that they are going to be sold for what they cost.
I quoted some of these figures purposely to show that they were sold for less than could have been realized for them by what one might consider businesslike methods.
^The Acting Chairman.]
We have also to take into consideration the important fact that some of this merchandise was never used and was sold at so much per ton. Some of it was sold since the statement I quoted was drawn up. This statement is dated March 31, 1945. Do those sales enter into the cost or profit of Polymer? We
want to know that.
/
This afternoon the minister chose to ignore the question which I happened to have on the order paper. He may have acted wisely. That is for him to say. But if we are to endorse the resolution to let any department of the government operate or continue to operate we are at least entitled to information, and I submit that we should have had a different answer. How are we to analyse a statement without having such information before us?
I understand that some of the new merchandise whicji was sold by the ton, and which forms the greater part of the amount quoted, was sent to another plant just below the Polymer Corporation. I do not know why, and my people wonder why, it was sent there to be loaded on cars instead of being loaded in the Polymer Corporation. I submit that these amounts which I quoted represent a realization of some 4-5 per cent of cost. I also appreciate that the government or some department of government could have a building in some faraway place which would have involved a considerable amount in dismantling, and the cost would probably be out of proportion to what it would have been worth when dismantled. But there is one point which my people question, and rightly so. We are not the only place in Canada which is hard up for housing, for toilets and wash-basins, for electrical wiring and so on. I do not mind telling this committee that considerably more than two or three million feet of good lumber could have been salvaged from these staff and bunkhouses, et cetera. It seems like poor business for the houses to remain there unused when the material could be used in erecting houses for veterans and others who need them.
It seems obvious that I am not permitted to put on record more details concerning these particular sales, but the few item? I have given come to a little better than three-quarters of a million dollars. In all probability, when these and other companies are investigated by the war expenditures committee there will be considerable doubt in the minds of reasonable people on both sides of the house as to whether or not it is good policy to endorse this resolution. As I see it, if I vote in favour of this particular resolution I am

Research Council
endorsing what the government has done. I tried to tell the committee, and I finally did what it had attempted to do. I submit in all sincerity that, on the record of what has taken place there and elsewhere, we ought to question whether it is a wise policy. Let me give an instance that they know about. Everybody is talking about this sort of thing, and this is what our people are restless about. An item involving some 822,000 was sold for about $2,000. It consisted of forms for building pavement. They would be just as good twenty-five years from now as they are to-day. Any contractor who knew they were to be sold or were for sale would have given, fifty, sixty or seventy per cent of the cost price. The only conclusion I can come to is that to which my constituents would come, namely, whether it is to be a wise policy to agree to -this, and whether they are to be secured not ' only there but wherever there is a crown corporation, if those crown corporations are to continue operating as they have done in the past.

I am going to discuss it, as my hon. friend discussed it a few moments ago. I am going to talk about it for a while, if I can have the attention of the committee. Be that as it may, perhaps I might deal with the reasonable part of my hon. friend's speech, brief though it was.
The hon. gentleman spoke of the fact that the Polymer Corporation is not liable for municipal taxes. That arises from a provision in the British North America Act whereby property of the crown is not taxable by provincial or municipal governments. The township knew that was the case when the industry located there. I received no objections from it at the time; in fact I had a very warm invitation to locate the plant in Sarnia, and we were very glad to do so because it seemed the reasonable point at which to establish the industry. The plant does pay for services; it pays a very substantial amount to the town of Sarnia and the township. My hon. friend mentioned $70,000 a year as a reasonable tax. Well, I believe the plant pays to the township or the city of Sarnia something like half that amount for services. But I would point out that, as a result of the government plant being constructed in its present location, private industry has located on adjoining property; and private industry is spending some five or six million dollars, with every prospect that this amount will be largely increased as the years go by. From the very nature of its operation, the Polymer plant will be the focal point of an organic chemical industry which uses the by-products of the Polymer operation. I think the town of Sarnia and the adjacent township will have no financial reason to regret that the Polymer Corporation has been established there.

I might explain that the item of $3 million is a reserve set-up to cover a liability created in connection with the purchase of crude rubber prior to the fall of Singapore. The government had, at the time, outstanding contracts for crude rubber. It was purchased f.o.b. docks, Singapore, and at the fall of Singapore the question arose as to how much of that rubber would be deliveredi, and how much liability would be set up in Singapore for rubber which we would not receive. Originally the reserve was something more than $5 million, that being the peak value of the commitments in Singapore.
At this time the rubber has been largely delivered. Some of it came in during the war-

Research Council
years. Some came in ships riddled wtih gunfire, but still afloat. A surprising amount of it was received even after the fall of Singapore. But there still remained a considerable amount of rubber unaccounted for, and the $3 million was maintained on the books to cover the complete liquidation of those liabilities.
Recently, other shipments of rubber have arrived from warehouse stocks in Singapore, and we have now determined that the S3 million item is much in excess of the actual liability.

subtopic: OPERATIONS AND FINANCING-SUPERANNUATION AND PENSION PROVISIONS, ETC.

speechtext: This free and easy way of dealing with interest does not seem to work out with what the minister said this afternoon about the advantages of the accounting methods of crown companies. speechtext:
Back in 1939, at the commencement of the war, the Fairmont company was organized, I believe as the second crown company, to stock-pile rubber and silk,

two commodities for which the government was dependent on foreign sources. Since it was impossible for private buyers to operate in the market, it was necessary for the government to take over the purchasing of all rubber and silk that were required for war purposes, or, in fact, for any purpose. The Fairmont company carried on its operations until 1943. At that time the Polymer Corporation was selling synthetic rubber and it seemed reasonable that that corporation should also take over the selling of crude rubber. Therefore, the name of the Fairmont company was changed to Polymer Sales and Service Limited.

Mr. HOWE,: It is a charge of the same nature. It has nothing to do with Polymer. It is a balancing item in the accounts of Polymer Sales. The explanation given in the auditor general's report is as follows:
This company (formerly Fairmont Company Limited) ceased business as of June 30, 1945. It acquired the stored crude and synthetic rubber and made sales thereof to manufacturers having contracts with the Crown for the production of war supplies, and to manufacturers engaged in essential civilian production.
As stated in paragraph 252 of last year's report, stocks of rubber were revalued upwards in 1943 to the equivalent of current replacement prices, and an offsetting inventory appreciation reserve established. Order in council P.C. 5750 of July 20, 1943, authorized the company to collect surcharges (based on tire deliveries) from the Department of National Defence and other organizations, for the proportion of rubber going
Research Council

into the production of war supplies, and also to collect from Commodity Prices Stabilization Corporation Limited amounts from time to time estimated for the loss incurred on the proportion of rubber going into the production of civilian goods.	.
It is clear to me, and I think I can make it clear to my hon. friend.

subtopic: OPERATIONS AND FINANCING-SUPERANNUATION AND PENSION PROVISIONS, ETC.
speechtext: That is not necessarily the same thing.

subtopic: OPERATIONS AND FINANCING-SUPERANNUATION AND PENSION PROVISIONS, ETC.
speechtext: My memory is perhaps helping me. I think I can explain it now. The Polymer Sales Corporation bought crude rubber where it could at the price it had to pay. It sold the rubber going into consumer goods at the ceiling price. The stabilization corporation objected to stabilizing rubber going into military goods. It said: We are responsible for the consumer but we are not responsible for the war, and therefore you must separate the crude rubber that goes into civilian goods from the crude rubber that goes into military uses. Therefore, after the total subsidy had been arrived at, it was divided into two items, one of which was paid by the stabilization corporation and the other by the Department of Munitions and Supply. One was called stabilization income, paid by the stabilization corporation, and the other was the war item, called surcharge income, which was paid by the Department of Munitions and Supply. But both covered the same item; that is, the difference between the purchase price of crude rubber and its sale at the ceiling price.

Something has been heard in this house about the iniquities of the government, and I have no doubt they are plentiful, in allegedly selling materials at very low prices. In the course of his speech when he introduced this resolution the minister said, as reported at page 1517 of Hansard:
I have yet to hear any businessman suggest it was not a good thing for Canadian business to have Canada's only source of rubber in the hands of the government, rather than in the hands of a private corporation.
I find myself in complete agreement with him on that statement, but why does he restrict himself to rubber alone? Are there not other materials equally necessary and valuable to Canada apart from rubber? One of them, one with which the government has had something to do, is magnesium. Although I support the principle of the resolution, I submit that the government ought to go farther in this matter of crown companies and take under its aegis or its wing those corporations which are dealing in a monopolistic way with materials that are vital to the welfare of Canada, one of which, as I have said, is magnesium. The history of this 'metal is interesting. At the end of the last war it cost $5 a pound in the United States and there were
Research Council

eight competing companies. Two years afterwards, there were only two competitors, one being the American Magnesium Corporation, a subsidiary of Aluminum Corporation, which I shall call Alcoa, and the other was the Dow Chemical company. For a number of years these two corporations were apparently in competition because the price fell to fifty-five cents a pound in 1927. Then the American Magnesium Corporation and the Dow Chemical company came to an agreement whereby they were going to split the market and sell the material on a certain basis at a certain price agreed to between themselves. One of the reasons for that was that the aluminum monopoly feared competition. It had invested millions of dollars in bauxite and did not want that investment imperiled by this new light metal, magnesium. The Department of Justice, as a matter of fact, ruled that the companies had agreed to keep the price of magnesium one-third higher than the price of aluminum, and in this connection I would quote from "Patents for Hitler" by Guenter Reimann, who, in turn, quotes Norman M. Little, assistant United States attorney-general, who made the following statement in a lecture delivered before the Indiana state bar association:
And so it is with a productive capacity in the aluminum industry inadequate to meet the numerous demands of the expanding airplane industry, we are also simultaneously confronted with a limited capacity for the manufacture of magnesium, the only competing metal! This is all the more appalling when it is realized that of the sources for magnesium, brine deposits and magnesite are plentiful in this country.
In Germany the nazis had realized to the full the value of magnesium. The price was exactly the same as that for aluminum, and realizing its value, the Germans in 1931 came to an agreement with Alcoa whereby the patents of Alcoa were pooled with the I. G. Farben company and there was formed the Magnesium Development company. That organization was formed, not for purposes of production, but with the object of holding patents. The only company which was granted a licence was the Dow Chemical company, and by special agreement production was limited. This, again, was private enterprise at work, ensuring for themselves the maximum profits, no matter what the danger was to the country.

The result of that policy was that at the beginning of the war German production exceeded United States production by ten times. The value of this metal is obvious when one considers that aluminum is a third as heavy as steel and magnesium half as heavy as aluminum. The government apparently decided that this was a necessary and vital metal for the war effort and started a plant at Haley's Station, and last year as will be found in sessional paper 241, I asked certain questions. I quote:
Was a new process for producing magnesium developed at thfe national research council? If so, who was responsible for this development?
The answer I received was:
An old process for the production of metallic magnesium was investigated by a private group and funds were provided by the group to have the process tested at the national research council laboratories. A small pilot plant was set up and out of this came improvements that were applied in the construction of the commercial plant. The work was done under the direction of Doctor Lloyd Pidgeon of the national research council staff and became known as the Pidgeon process.
I next asked:
Was a crown company formed to exploit this development in Canada?
The answer was:
No. Dominion Magnesium Limited was formed by the original group of parties interested and acquired a deposit of dolomite near Haley's Station, Ontario, in an area where power was available.
After investigation of the cost of the erection of a plant to produce magnesium in Canada, the capital cost for the required production rate was found to be lowest by using the Pidgeon process so the minister of the Department of Munitions and Supply entered into an agreement with the Dominion Magnesium Limited to design, construct and operate a plant on the property near Haley's Station, Ontario. The supervision of the work was carried out under Wartime Metals Corporation starting in April, 1942.
The cost of the plant to the dominion government to produce this material was $3,464,102.15. Afterwards, we got rid of it to this company for $1,400,000. I am going to suggest to the minister that he consider very

Research Council
seriously the advisability of taking this plant over again on the basis that what it is producing is vital for Canada, not only in war time but also in peace time, and also in view of the fact that there is no guarantee at all that the new company will not enter into some cartel arrangements with foreign countries to the detriment of Canadian trade.
In the Financial Post of May 18 it is stated that a new marketing agreement has been completed by the company with Swedish interests and that a similar agreement is in process of being completed shortly with interests in Belgium. The wording may be unfortunate, but at least it smacks too much of the cartel arrangements which have been made in the past.
Now a word about the Aluminum Corporation, which is also another monopoly in this country and which, therefore, should be government-owned and controlled. A debate has already been held in this house on more than one occasion when the charge was made that aluminum was a monopoly. I believe there was an investigation into the matter by a committee, and the committee tried to whitewash the corporation. They did not succeed. The United States department of justice showed that it was a monopoly, and so it is. The danger of monopoly is that the men who run it are more interested in making profits for themselves than in looking after the interests of the country. That, I think, can be easily seen from the senate inquiry in the United States. Again I quote, and this time Mr. Thurman Arnold, who appeared before the patents committee where he was asked some questions about Alcoa's monopoly. The charge had been made that when this great monopolistic corporation knew processes had been discovered which threatened to impair the capital of the company, it had bought the processes and filed them away, thus not making them available for the benefit of the nation as a whole.
Thurman Arnold stated:
To Alcoa's monopoly, the use of the processes covered by those patents would have been disastrous, for its monopoly is basically a monopoly control of bauxite resources; its control of processing and fabricating facilities would have been much easier for a competitor to challenge. As a result, when a potential competitor appeared in this country with the Haglund patents for making aluminum from something besides bauxite they finally reached an agreement with him on a very remunerative basis. He received, I believe, about a million dollars and employment as a consultant at a fancy figure. The process never went into production; and Alcoa only recently was referring to the processes as "experimental," although we are informed that Italy has had them in production since 1928.
To add further to the patriotism of these great monopolies I would call to the attention of the committee the case of Mr. Arthur Bunker, who was the chief of the aluminum and magnesium section of the OPM, one of the dollar-a-year men. It was his task to preside over this section and, although the United States government provided funds for financing new plants, there was extraordinary difficulty in getting these funds used. Protests were made continually to the government that no additional aluminum plants were made because the same Mr. Arthur Bunker who was getting a dollar a year from the government was also getting 860,000 a year from the Lehman Corporation, which had a large investment in aluminum shares. These are only two examples of monopoly in this country which ought to come under government control, and I can think of no better method than that of the crown corporation. May I commend that to the attention of the minister, especially in view of his statement which I again repeat:
I have 3'et to hear any businessman suggest it was not a good thing for Canadian business to have Canada's only source of rubber in the hands of the government, rather than in the hands of a private corporation.
If that is good for one monopoly it is good for others.

All these questions can be asked, but for myself I am saying that I cannot work up any particular enthusiasm about government going into business, and I do not care what government it is. Of course there is some little excuse for the government to be in business in time of war. That is a time of emergency when certain freedoms have to give way to a type of regimentation, a type of control, because there is a specific job to be done. I am going to compliment the minister; I think I can do that without going too far as a member of the opposition, in saying that during the war he did a fair job in bringing this country into the full-time productive effort that was required. But since the war has ended some of us have been looking for some of these controls to be loosened up a little and dropped off. Sometimes I wonder if the minister has not just a little bit of a mania for wanting a finger in a great many pies. Whether he has or not, I do not know, but I do not want him or any minister to become a sort of czar of government business.
Sometimes these government corporations start quite innocently. Their intentions are good. I might refer to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation which was innocently brought into existence to see that the Canadian public got good radio free from abuses, and so on. But over the years that corporation has gradually taken to itself tremendous authority, and has practically become a radio monopoly in Canada. I deplore that.
There is something else with respect to government corporations, and it is this. They do not necessarily have to operate at a profit; they can operate at a loss. Let us recognize that. Let no one say that I am in favour of

exorbitant profiteering, but government corporations do not have to operate efficiently by reason of the fact that they must make both ends meet. If they do not; if they show a loss, the government can say, "Well, we always have the taxpayer to rely upon to make up any deficiencies," so the public pays just the same. I believe that in the minds of the Canadian people to-day there exists a desire gradually to do away with controls. The present administration may put on a bold front and say, "Gradually we are going to do away with these controls." But if, in place of these controls, they set up huge government corporations with power to regulate business, then the effect of controls is there just the same. I need only refer again, as an example, to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. It is supposed to be in the competitive field of radio; yet it makes the rules and regulations. By reason of special authority given to it under the act, it controls radio in Canada; and no fooling. There is nothing to say that ultimately any government corporation cannot do the same thing in its own line of business. I believe in private enterprise.

I think it is, and I like to be a good commonsense man. I do not believe private enterprise has any right to license. I believe there is a place where, by legislation rather than controls, by law, private enterprise can be governed according to statute. I believe private business itself should be alarmed at the trend of things to-day in this country and in the world. It is all very well to say that we must have government corporations to combat monopolies; but, generally speaking, when government corporations come into existence they become monopolies, and monopolies under the state. Private business has need to be alarmed at that trend.
I am going to suggest, too, that labour should be alarmed. Perhaps on the face of it that may sound strange, but the more the government goes into business, the less freedom labour will have. Let them recognize that.

I am going to advance one further thought, because I believe that government in business affects parliament in the sense that parliament has been regarded as a legislative body. Members of parliament have been regarded as legislators. But it seems to me that parliament has become and is more and more becoming an administrative body, and that, instead of members being legislators, they are fast becoming government agents. The more government goes into business, the more legislators become agents and, if they are on the government side, apologists for what the government is doing, while if they are on the opposition side they become perhaps business critics, when we should be laying a legislative foundation upon which business, people and the country itself can be free and enjoy the liberties of mankind that our democracy, if it is effective at all, can offer the country. I think we are all cognizant of the fact that parliament is beginning to fall into disrepute in this country. The public are beginning to feel that we are dilly-dallying. The public are beginning to feel that we are dealing with a lot of non-essentials, trivial things, when there are such big issues in the world to deal with. I say that because I believe that the more the government go into business, the more critical we have to be of the dollars and cents they may spend, or the amount they may make here, or the individual who may be employed here, or the authority given to somebody over there. To my mind, it is all a matter of private and individual liberty.
Let us be legislators, creating a legislative foundation upon which the country can build a real, effective and free democracy, where the people themselves will enjoy to the fullest extent all that Canada can offer them.
I cannot work up any great enthusiasm for the measure, because I do not know where it will lead us. I do not agree with the principle of the government in business.

When the resolution was before the committee on the last occasion the minister indicated, as will be found at page 1512 of Hansard, that he would be willing to table financial statements of any of these corporations which are to be continued. Will he be good enough to submit to the committee the financial statements of Wartime Housing Limited and Research Enterprises Limited? Those are two in which I am particularly interested.

subtopic: OPERATIONS AND FINANCING-SUPERANNUATION AND PENSION PROVISIONS, ETC.
speechtext: All the balance sheets are published in the public accounts for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1945.

subtopic: OPERATIONS AND FINANCING-SUPERANNUATION AND PENSION PROVISIONS, ETC.
speechtext: I have seen the public accounts, but I take it that when the minister made his offer he meant that he was prepared to bring before the committee a financial statement that was completely up to date in in each case. The information contained in the public accounts is now fourteen months old'.

subtopic: OPERATIONS AND FINANCING-SUPERANNUATION AND PENSION PROVISIONS, ETC.
speechtext: I have statements which -have been furnished me, but unfortunately they have not been audited. I would be glad to give the information contained therein, but I would hesitate to table as a financial statement anything that the auditor general has not had an opportunity to audit.

subtopic: OPERATIONS AND FINANCING-SUPERANNUATION AND PENSION PROVISIONS, ETC.
speechtext: Probably the minister would make them open to inspection by members?

subtopic: OPERATIONS AND FINANCING-SUPERANNUATION AND PENSION PROVISIONS, ETC.
speechtext: Certainly.

subtopic: OPERATIONS AND FINANCING-SUPERANNUATION AND PENSION PROVISIONS, ETC.
speechtext: This afternoon reference was made by the minister to the desirability of referring the annual statements of crown corporations to a standing committee of the house. Does he propose to provide in the bill that these statements shall be tabled in parliament? Will he indicate, also whether the government intends to take steps either to set up a committee to review these statements or to clothe some standing committee with power to do so?

subtopic: OPERATIONS AND FINANCING-SUPERANNUATION AND PENSION PROVISIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
It would hardly be appropriate for me to instruct parliament as to what it should do with a report or with a bill. Any

Research Council
member of parliament can ask that a bill be referred to a committee of the house. I have suggested that I thought it would be appropriate to refer these statements of crown companies to a committee. At the present time they are referred to the war expenditures committee, and1 I suggested that perhaps an appropriate committee would be the committee on railways and shipping, government owned. I would welcome any suggestion from hon. members as to an appropriate committee.

subtopic: OPERATIONS AND FINANCING-SUPERANNUATION AND PENSION PROVISIONS, ETC.
speechtext: There is a point which arises out of the statement appearing in the press to-day concerning the new order issued by the government, under which control of Wartime Housing Limited and veterans housing will be lodged in the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. Will the minister indicate what bearing this will have upon the operations of Wartime Housing Limited, because that is a crown corporation to which the minister has referred several times during the course of the deliberations on this resolution. He indicated that this corporation would probably carry on for two or three years, but that it was not intended to be carried on indefinitely.

subtopic: OPERATIONS AND FINANCING-SUPERANNUATION AND PENSION PROVISIONS, ETC.
speechtext: I think my hon. friend has answered himself. The company is brought under the aegis of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. Eventually, when it becomes purely an administrative company, its functions will be merged with those of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. While it remains a building company, it will continue to operate as a separate identity and will, perhaps, absorb some of the work at present being carried on by other building agencies of the government. For example, it will probably be the contractor for emergency housing, which now functions under the control of the Central Mortgage and1 Housing Corporation.

subtopic: OPERATIONS AND FINANCING-SUPERANNUATION AND PENSION PROVISIONS, ETC.
speechtext: Does the government contemplate introducing further legislation along that line which would define the relationship of Wartime Housing Limited to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, or of the minister's department to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation? Under the 1945 legislation which set up the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, the corporation was placed under the administration of the Minister1 of Finance, but by an order in council passed a month ago it was transferred to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply. Is it the intention of the government to introduce legislation in that respect at this session?

subtopic: OPERATIONS AND FINANCING-SUPERANNUATION AND PENSION PROVISIONS, ETC.
speechtext: Consideration is being given to certain amendments to the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation Act.

subtopic: OPERATIONS AND FINANCING-SUPERANNUATION AND PENSION PROVISIONS, ETC.
speechtext: At this session?

subtopic: OPERATIONS AND FINANCING-SUPERANNUATION AND PENSION PROVISIONS, ETC.
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: OPERATIONS AND FINANCING-SUPERANNUATION AND PENSION PROVISIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
I wish to ask two or three questions which perhaps might better be defined as suggestions. In the meantime I cannot overlook the amazing support given to the principle of this bill, in which I join, by my hon. friends over here. I had occasion to say last fall that they are anxious for the socialization of everything, and they are in great support of the minister on this particular occasion. I noticed they put in their oar and then immediately went away because no doubt they had more important things to do than listen to the minister's answers.
My first problem, my first question and my first suggestion is this: When the minister considers creating a crown corporation will he not consider bringing it within the orbit of a separate bill? He has suggested three corporations, Polymer, Eldorado and Arsenals. I know the minister will realize that I am not attributing anything wrong to him because, from the best information I get, he is going to leave the government on October 31. I cannot see any connection in discussion between Polymer, Arsenals and Eldorado. I know that any schoolteacher would immediately say to me, "Are you so dumb that you cannot separate those things in argument?" I confess that I am that dumb. What I have in mind is that once we get a bill which generalizes about crown corporations it is a very simple thing to bring in a little amendment for one or two more or, as the minister said to-day, maybe twenty.

subtopic: OPERATIONS AND FINANCING-SUPERANNUATION AND PENSION PROVISIONS, ETC.
speechtext: We had thirty-one at one time. We are cutting them down to five, and I do not think it will ever be any more than five.

subtopic: OPERATIONS AND FINANCING-SUPERANNUATION AND PENSION PROVISIONS, ETC.
speechtext: But you said it might be twenty. There are some wonderful expressions of speech such as hyperbole and literative harmony. I do not know what that last one means, and I am inclined to think my schoolteacher friend over here who accuses us of not being farmers will know exactly what that figure of speech means.

subtopic: OPERATIONS AND FINANCING-SUPERANNUATION AND PENSION PROVISIONS, ETC.
speechtext: You had all of nine to vote for your amendment.

subtopic: OPERATIONS AND FINANCING-SUPERANNUATION AND PENSION PROVISIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
I am just going to say a word or two to the hon. gentleman for Winnipeg North, and I use the word "gentleman" advisedly because he is a very good friend of mine, who last spoke. His position is this: He will go anywhere with anybody who will create socialism. He recog-
Research Council

nizes us in this group as his enemies. God bless them; let him keep on thinking that because, for the first time in his life, he is right, He is one of those theorists, one of those people who know all about architecture but who have never built anything. He is one of those persons who know all about bridges but never did anything but swim under them. So that I thoroughly understand his position. Nevertheless he is one of the most delightful men this House of Commons ever saw, because he has such wonderful idealism. It is an amazing thing that he has never run up against a few practical facts.
May I suggest to the minister that in bringing in bills or resolutions for the forma-ation of crown companies he bring in one at a time? I am all for the principle of the research council spreading its wings and doing a great deal, but why cannot we deal with one thing at a time? I and my hon. friends to my left differ fundamentally on the principle of doing business. I believe in a principle. I believe in the research council. I believe in its expansion, but I cannot understand why the minister should suggest that blanket authority be given to the research council to form corporations. The minister mentioned one thing. He said, with respect to patents owned by the corporation, that they should be sold at the price the market would bear, and I go with him. But why you should require a corporation to do that business is utterly beyond me. Will the minister not now say what things he wants corporate authority for? If you have a patent to sell you can put an ad in the newspapers and ask for tenders. You do not need a corporation to do that simple thing.
Let me make a comparison between these crown companies and the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, which is also a crown company. I tried for several days in the house to find out whether the broadcasting corporation had bought one and a half million dollars of equipment. I tried to find out whether they intended to take over certain wave lengths belonging to three stations, one in Toronto, one in Winnipeg and one in Calgary. I was stupid, if you will, but I was persistent, as most stupid people are, and the Minister of National Revenue, who is not in his seat to-night-told me that he did not know whether these things had been done or not. I then asked the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply, and he told me that he would accept my question as a notice. Of course I knew they had sent out word a month before to these stations that they were going to take over their wave lengths. Why could we not have been told that in the House of

Commons? It is easy to say that these corporations can be reviewed before the House of Commons, but let us see just what can happen. The act setting up the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation provides that the corporation may not spend more than $10,000 without the approval of council and that they may not order anything costing over $10,000 without the approval of council-but we now learn that they have ordered material to a value of $1,500,000.
Do not let anyone think I am suggesting for a moment that the gentlemen who are put in charge of these corporations are not honest. Let us admit that they are, but power begets power. I am going to say something about the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply which I hope he will accept as a compliment. There is a chap named Petrillo in the United States who looks after musicians and they are going to pay him $400 a week for what? For one hour's work a week. The Minister of Reconstruction and Supply and Petrillo are both .drunk with power. So do not let these corporations get away from us. I think the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply is the most honourable man I know, but Petrillo is a rotter and a crook. I am not comparing them in that way at all because they are as the polea apart.
